records.toxicity_detail: Source: NC State Extension Plant Toolbox, Anthurium scherzerianum page. Severity: the page states "This plant has low severity poison characteristics" and its "Poisonous to Humans" block gives Poison Severity: Low; that block is human-scoped. Poison Symptoms (as written): "If ingested, oral irritation, pain and swelling of mouth, tongue, and lips, excessive drooling, vomiting, and difficulty swallowing. The sap can cause skin or eye irritation upon contact." Poison Toxic Principle: Insoluble calcium oxalates. Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes. Poison Part (full list): Flowers, Fruits, Leaves, Roots, Sap/Juice, Seeds, Stems. In its Landscape group the page's Problems field (separate from Resistance To Challenges, which lists only Humidity) lists Contact Dermatitis, Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Cats, Problem for Children, Problem for Dogs (the cat and dog scope comes from the Problem for Cats / Problem for Dogs values, not from the human-scoped Poison block). The Insects, Diseases, and Other Plant Problems prose says: "If ingested, this plant is toxic for pets and humans." (pets unspecified by animal in that sentence). Page tags also include #poisonous, #poisonous if ingested, #contact dermatitis, #problem for children, #problem for dogs, #problem for cats; Plant Type field lists Herbaceous Perennial, Houseplant, Perennial, Poisonous. Only one admissible source was reachable, so no scope disagreement could be assessed.
unknowns: Only NC State Plant Toolbox (plants.ces.ncsu.edu) loaded for this exact taxon. RHS had no page at the guessed slug and its search is script-rendered; Missouri Botanical Garden pages failed to connect (ConnectError/ProxyError), and plantfinder.mobot.org and ask.ifas.ufl.edu were not reachable from the sandbox. UF/IFAS EDIS and Clemson HGIC were not found for this species. No cross-source corroboration or disagreement check was possible.

is_edible=false is based only on NC State's statement that the plant is toxic if ingested; no source addresses use as food.

chill_damage_f left null: NC State says 'It prefers temperatures of 60 degrees Fahrenheit or above' (a preference, not a damage-onset figure) and gives USDA zones 10-12 (a survival range). Day/night temperature ranges are not stated.
humidity_need=high is read from NC State's 'warm and humid conditions' preference; no percentage given. The page also tags the plant 'humidity tolerant'.

Soil: NC State says 'moist well-drained soil' and tags Good Drainage + Moist (mapped to moderate), and 'Light and airy soil is required', but names no potting-mix type, so soil_base is null. Soil pH null: NC State shows Acid (<6.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0) bands only (open-ended floor; no second source to check a ceiling).

water_regime=dry_surface_between is from 'water when the soil is dry to the touch'; the same page also wants 'moist' soil and warns 'Overwatering can lead to root rot'. No day intervals or probe depth stated, so left null.

Light: NC State says 'medium to high indirect sunlight' and 'Direct sunlight can scorch the leaves'; no foot-candle or direct-sun-hour figure is species-specific (the 2-6 hours appears only inside the generic Partial Shade category label), so those are null. outdoor_sun_exposure part_shade is from the structured Light field 'Partial Shade'.
Fertilizer: NC State only says high-phosphorus fertilizer encourages blooms; no interval, season or dilution stated.

Pollinator attraction not stated on the page (null). Mature size is from NC State's Dimensions block (Height 1 ft 0 in - 1 ft 6 in = 12-18 in; Width 0 ft 6 in - 1 ft 0 in = 6-12 in); the description prose says 'up to about 1.5 feet tall and 1 foot wide'.
This record is kept separate from Anthurium andraeanum (landed as 'Anthurium'); no content was borrowed from it.

records.toxicity_detail: Source: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox page for Begonia masoniana. Under its "Poisonous to Humans:" block (human-scoped heading): Poison Severity: Low. Poison Symptoms, as written: "Kidney failure (in grazing animals), vomiting, salivation in dogs/cats. The most toxic part is the underground roots. The sap may cause skin irritation." So vomiting and salivation are scoped to dogs/cats, and kidney failure is scoped to grazing animals, not dogs/cats. Poison Toxic Principle: Soluble calcium oxalates. Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes. Poison Part: Roots, Sap/Juice. Problems tags (separate from the Poison block): Contact Dermatitis, Problem for Cats, Problem for Children, Problem for Dogs, Problem for Horses. Tags line: #houseplant #interesting leaves #interiorscape #winter interest #problem for dogs #problem for horses #problem for cats #showy leaves #warm climates #indoor #black walnut toxicity tolerant #container plant #hortcontest. Plant Type: Herbaceous Perennial, Houseplant. No other admissible source was found for this exact species, so there is no disagreement to disclose.
records.water_dry_down_target: surface of the soil nearly dry before adding water (stated for when active growth slows; during growth, keep evenly moist)
unknowns: Only the NC State page was found and verified for this exact species. No dedicated RHS, Missouri Botanical Garden, UF/IFAS, Clemson, Penn State, UMD or UGA page for Begonia masoniana was located (an RHS search returned no masoniana hit; MoBot and EDIS searches could not be loaded), so every populated field rests on a single source.

name_note is null: NC State's Common Name(s) list has a single entry, Iron Cross Begonia, and no admissible source disagrees. scientific_name_accepted comes from NC State's page binomial, not an RHS Name Status check.

toxic_to_pets is true on the NC State wording 'vomiting, salivation in dogs/cats' plus the Problem for Cats and Problem for Dogs tags. Severity Low comes from NC State's 'Poisonous to Humans:' block, which is human-scoped, not from the pet tags. Kidney failure is scoped to grazing animals only.

chill_damage_f left null: NC State says the plant 'will not survive outdoors in temperatures below 55 degrees F' and is hardy to USDA zones 11 and 12. That is a survival and hardiness statement, not a stated damage-onset figure.
day_f and night_f left null: NC State says only 'preferring temperatures in the low 70s', with no day/night split or range. cool_rest_note is null because no source addresses a cool rest.

direct_sun_hours_max and light_fc left null: NC State's Light field renders 'Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)'; the category Partial Shade is species-specific, but the '2-6 hours' parenthetical is the site-wide category definition, and the species prose says only 'bright but indirect or filtered light' with no footcandle or hour figure. outdoor_sun_exposure part_shade reflects the Partial Shade category; the plant is hardy only in zones 11-12, so it is chiefly an indoor plant.

soil_drainage moderate is a judgment from NC State's Soil Drainage tags 'Good Drainage' and 'Occasionally Dry' plus the prose 'moisture retentive potting mix'. Fast was deliberately not used. The tags do not include an occasionally-wet value.

water_regime keep_moist reflects the growth-period instruction 'keep evenly moist'. NC State qualifies it in the same paragraph: when growth slows, let the soil surface nearly dry, and the plant 'must not be overwatered'. The Occasionally Dry drainage tag points the same way, so a dry_surface_between reading is also defensible. No interval in days is stated, so the water_*_days_est fields are null.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max left null: NC State lists 'Acid (<6.0)' and 'Neutral (6.0-8.0)'. The acid band is open-ended, and no RHS pH field was available to check a ceiling against the neutral band.
humidity_pct_min and humidity_pct_max are null: NC State says only that the plant prefers high humidity, with no percentage figure.

Fertilizer schedule, strength and active months: NC State's page does not address fertilizing. is_edible and attracts_pollinators: the page does not address eating, and carries no Attracts field. All left null.
NC State's Soil Texture (High Organic Matter) and Landscape Location (Container, Houseplants) fields are not used for any schema field beyond what is cited.

records.name_note: NC State's rendered Common Name(s) list gives Alligator Fern first, then Crocodile Fern. Its Description opens "The crocodile fern is a tropical epiphyte fern" and says the textured fronds resemble crocodile skin, "hence, its common name." MoBot's Noteworthy Characteristics calls crocodile fern "the sometimes used common name". Former names per NC State's "Previously known as" list: Drynaria musifolia, Pleopeltis musifolia, Polypodium musifolium. NC State lists the cultivar Crocodyllus, and MoBot's Noteworthy Characteristics says the plant may be sold under the cultivar name Crocodylus. This is the catalog's first Microsorum. Crocodile Fern is used as common_name because NC State's Description opens with it and names it the plant's common name; Alligator Fern, first in NC State's two-item list, appears in neither source's prose.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's page for this exact taxon carries the tags #non-toxic for cats and #non-toxic for dogs in its Tags block (co-listed with #fern, #houseplant, #epiphytic, #herbaceous perennial and others). The page has no Poison section, symptom list, poison part or handling warning. MoBot's page for this taxon says nothing about toxicity, so only one admissible source addresses it and none disagrees.
records.water_dry_down_target: soil surface begins to feel dry
unknowns: No RHS page for the species Microsorum musifolium was found (only a cultivar page, which is not admissible for the species), so RHS Name Status, RHS size and RHS hardiness are absent; scientific_name_accepted rests on the NC State and MoBot dedicated pages.
MoBot Plant Finder was read through a browser because the page cache fetcher cannot reach plantfinder.mobot.org; its quotes may report SKIP in verify_quotes.
Clemson HGIC returned 403 and its Indoor Ferns factsheet is a multi-species page, so it was not used. No UF/IFAS, Penn State, Maryland or UGA page for this exact taxon was found.
toxic_to_pets=false rests on NC State's two tags only (#non-toxic for cats, #non-toxic for dogs). MoBot is silent on toxicity. NC State has no Poison block for this plant.

Temperature: NC State says the plant thrives between 60 to 75 degrees Fahrenheit without distinguishing day from night, so day_f and night_f are null. chill_damage_f 50 comes from NC State's 'Avoid exposure to temperatures below 50 degrees Fahrenheit'; MoBot says 'Plants generally dislike temperatures that dip below 50 degrees F.' NC State's USDA zones 10a-11b are a hardiness range, not used as damage onset.
Humidity: both sources say high humidity but give no percentage; NC State also says brown leaf edges indicate low humidity or tap water.

Watering: NC State says water when the soil surface begins to feel dry (dry_surface_between). MoBot's structured Water field reads Medium (mid-scale, disclosed as a counterpoint) and MoBot advises avoiding excess water at the roots. NC State warns overwatering can cause root rot. No numeric watering interval or check depth is stated, so those fields are null.

Fertilizer: NC State says a diluted half strength balanced liquid fertilizer once a month during spring and summer, and MoBot says fertilize monthly or use slow release. Month-based cadence and named seasons were not converted into a day interval or calendar months, so those fields are null.
Soil pH: NC State lists both Acid (<6.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0) bands; the Acid band is open-ended and RHS was unavailable to check the alkaline side, so both pH bounds are null.

Light: NC State's structured Light field lists Deep shade and Partial Shade (mapped to full_shade and part_shade); MoBot's prose says best sited in shady areas with bright indirect light. NC State says leaves scorch in direct sunlight but gives no hours, so direct_sun_hours_max and light_fc are null.

Size: NC State gives Height 1 ft. 0 in. - 3 ft. 0 in. and Width 1 ft. 0 in. - 3 ft. 0 in. (12-36 in.). MoBot's structured Height and Spread read 1.00 to 2.00 feet, narrower than NC State; NC State is the anchor per the size rule.
The plant is non-flowering, and neither source addresses edibility or pollinators, so is_edible and attracts_pollinators are null.

Read on MoBot's page by the researcher but not cited (MoBot refuses non-browser clients on this machine, so verify_quotes cannot check a new MoBot quote): MoBot's structured Common Name field reads 'microsorum', a genus label rather than a lead common name, and its Noteworthy Characteristics also gives Polypodium musifolium as a synonym. The audit asked for both in name_note; they are disclosed here instead.

records.name_note: NC State's dedicated page for Chlorophytum orchidastrum leads its rendered Common Name(s) list (alphabetized: Fire Flash, Fire Glory, Green Orange Spider Plant, Mandarin Plant, Mandarin Spider Plant, Sierra Leone Lily) with 'Fire Flash'; its H1 is the binomial only, and its Description prose opens with 'The green orange spider plant'. Fire Flash is used as common_name as the first item of that list. NC State lists Chlorophytum macropodum under 'Previously known as'. UF/IFAS publishes its guideline for 'Fire Flash' under the name Chlorophytum amaniense and describes an East African (Usambara Mountains, Tanzania) origin, whereas NC State gives the origin as West Tropical Africa to Zambia; the binomial recorded here follows NC State's dedicated page and the given name.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's page for this exact species carries the tags '#non-toxic for cats' and '#non-toxic for dogs' in its tag list (full tag list as rendered: #non-toxic for cats #non-toxic for dogs #clumping #partial shade tolerant #houseplant #herbaceous perennial #low maintenance #humidity tolerant #summer flowers #interesting leaves #container plant #erect #easy to grow houseplant). Its Plant Type field lists Herbaceous Perennial and Houseplant. The page has no Poison block, no symptom list, no poison-part list and no handling warning, and states no human-toxicity rating. The cat/dog statement is NC State's tag only; no second admissible source was found for this species.

unknowns: Only one admissible page for this exact name was found (NC State, plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/chlorophytum-orchidastrum/). RHS and MoBot pages for C. orchidastrum or C. amaniense were not found (RHS returned 404 on the guessed URLs; plantfinder.mobot.org was unreachable/denied in the sandbox), and Clemson's page is for C. comosum only and was not used.

A UF/IFAS EDIS publication (EP253) covers 'Fire Flash' under the binomial Chlorophytum amaniense and calls it a cultivar of that species with a Tanzanian origin. Because it is a different binomial and cultivar-framed, none of its care figures (light, temperature, fertilizer, chilling) were used for this orchidastrum record; it is cited only for the naming discrepancy.

NC State says the plant 'prefers moderate temperatures above 60 degrees Fahrenheit' and must be protected from freezing and lists zones 10b to 12b; this is a preference and a hardiness range, not a stated damage-onset temperature, so chill_damage_f, day and night temperature ranges are left null.
humidity_need left null: NC State gives 'a humid environment between 50 to 60%' (percent range recorded) and a 'humidity tolerant' tag, but no source states low/average/high.

direct_sun_hours_max left null: NC State's Light field reads "Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)", whose hour range is the site-wide category legend, not species prose. The species prose says they "thrive in bright, indirect light" and warns "Scorched leaves can occur from direct sunlight." Neither gives an hour figure. light_fc_min and light_fc_good have no admissible figure.
soil_ph_max left null: NC State's 'Neutral (6.0-8.0)' band gives a closed top, but no RHS pH field could be checked for alkaline tolerance.

soil_base standard_potting is read from NC State's well-drained loamy soil and perlite/sand potting-mix prose; the page names no specific commercial mix. soil_drainage moderate follows NC State's Good Drainage plus Moist pair.

No fertilizer, edibility or pollinator information found on the NC State page (no Attracts field), so those fields are null. Day-interval watering estimates left null: NC State frames watering only as the top-1-inch dry test.

Toxicity: NC State's non-toxic cat and dog tags are the only toxicity evidence; there is no Poison block or human-toxicity rating on the page. The page also warns of root rot and says to avoid overwatering.

records.name_note: Sources split on the lead common name. RHS's dedicated page pairs the binomial with baby sage (its H1 reads 'Salvia microphylla' and the rendered common-name line under the heading reads baby sage). NC State's dedicated page lists, in its stacked Common Name(s) list, Baby Sage, Blackcurrant Sage, Graham's Sage, Little Leaf Sage (alphabetized), while its Description opens with 'Little leaf sage'. Baby Sage was chosen because it is RHS's common name and first in NC State's list; Little Leaf Sage is NC State's prose name. NC State records the former name Salvia grahamii.
records.toxicity_detail: No admissible page gives a poison block or any cat/dog/human toxicity statement for this species. NC State's eating-related statements address the leaves only: its Edibility field reads 'Leaves have a scent of blackcurrant and can be used fresh or dried as a flavoring in an herbal tea,' (ending in a comma as rendered), its Description says 'The leaves are aromatic and can be used in making teas.', and its Leaf Description reads 'Green, almost triangular, toothed edges, edible, aromatic.' Other plant parts are not addressed.
unknowns: No Missouri Botanical Garden page could be confirmed: plantfinder.mobot.org refuses non-browser fetches and a web search surfaced no dedicated Salvia microphylla page. Clemson HGIC, UF/IFAS, Penn State, UMD and UGA turned up only genus-level or multi-species pages, which are not usable, so the record rests on NC State and RHS only.

Woody habit as given: NC State's Description calls it an evergreen shrub, but the same page's Woody Plant Leaf Characteristics field says Deciduous, its Plant Type field has two values (Perennial, Shrub), and its tags say tender perennial. RHS says Foliage Evergreen and rates hardiness H4 (UK scale). NC State lists USDA zones 7a-10b only. These conflict and no schema field holds them.

toxic_to_pets left null: no admissible page addresses toxicity to cats, dogs or humans; not inferred from the genus. is_houseplant is false: no admissible page addresses indoor culture, NC State's Plant Type field is Perennial, Shrub and its USDA zones run 7a-10b (the research record left it null; set false at landing).
is_edible is conditional on the plant part: NC State supports only the leaves, as a fresh or dried herbal-tea flavoring. Culinary claims were not carried over from common sage (S. officinalis).

records.name_note: Admissible sources lead with different common names. NC State's Common Name(s) list is alphabetized (Greek Valerian, then Jacob's Ladder) and its Description opens with "Jacob's ladder". RHS's subtitle for the dedicated Polemonium reptans page leads with "creeping Jacob's ladder" and lists Greek valerian among its Other common names. common_name follows the RHS subtitle form. MoBot's page could not be read in this run.
unknowns: MoBot (www.missouribotanicalgarden.org / plantfinder.mobot.org) could not be read: both hosts failed TLS certificate verification (unable to get local issuer certificate) in this run, so no MoBot page was consulted and nothing is cited from it. Fields MoBot might have supplied (water, pH, sun hours, size, toxicity) are left null or taken only from NC State and RHS.

toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail left null: neither the NC State page for Polemonium reptans (no Poison block, no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tags) nor the RHS page (no toxicity field) names any toxicity for this species. No toxicity was borrowed from P. caeruleum or the genus.
is_edible left null: no readable admissible source addresses eating this plant.

NC State and RHS give no onset temperature for cold damage, so chill_damage_f is null. Hardiness is not a schema field and is recorded here as given: NC State USDA zones 3a through 8b and NC Region Mountains and Piedmont; its Description says the plant does not tolerate the hot, humid conditions of the lower Piedmont and coastal plains. RHS rates it H7 (UK ratings).

water_regime left null: NC State has no watering statement, only a habitat note (moist deciduous woods and stream banks) and a drought-tolerance trait (low drought tolerance, goes dormant in drought), neither of which counts. RHS's structured Moisture field reads 'Moist but well-drained', which is a soil description and was used only for soil_drainage. water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm and the day-interval fields are null because this is an in-ground perennial and no source frames watering that way.

soil_drainage moderate comes from RHS's Moisture field 'Moist but well-drained'. NC State's Soil Drainage is a bare 'Good Drainage' (no moisture pair), which does not conflict. RHS's Cultivation sentence about fertile moist but well-drained soil was not used because it may be genus-level text.

soil_base garden_bed rests on RHS's suggested planting locations (Cottage and informal garden; Flower borders and beds). NC State's Soil Texture is Loam (Silt), but its Landscape Location list does include Container alongside Meadow, Naturalized Area, Riparian, Slope/Bank and Woodland, so container culture is not ruled out.
soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max left null: NC State gives no pH, and RHS's pH field reads 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral', so no numeric floor or ceiling is supported.

outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State's Light field lists Full sun and Partial Shade, and its tags say full sun tolerant and partial shade tolerant. RHS Position lists Full sun, Partial shade. The two agree. NC State's Description adds that it appreciates part shade. direct_sun_hours_max is null because the only hour figures are NC State's site-wide light legend.

Size sources differ. mature_height_in 12-36 and mature_spread_in 18-36 come from NC State's Dimensions block (1-3 ft tall, 1 ft 6 in to 3 ft wide). RHS gives Max Height 0.5-1 metres (19.7-39.4 in) and Max Spread 0.1-0.5 metres (3.9-19.7 in), a narrower spread, with Time to Maturity 2-5 years. NC State was used as the anchor.

Synonyms differ by source. NC State lists previously known as Polemonium quadriflorum, Polemonium reptans var. reptans and var. villosum. RHS lists the synonym Polemonium pulchellum Salisb. and Name Status Correct for Polemonium reptans.
No light_fc, humidity, temperature-range or fertilizer data exist in the admissible sources for this garden perennial, so those fields are null.
Greek Valerian (NC State's common name) is a different plant from Red Valerian (Valeriana rubra). The sibling Polemonium caeruleum was not used for any field.
